newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zairean rebels push within 150 km of Kinshasa.
newsitem.headline: Zairean rebels push within 150 km of Kinshasa.

text.p: Zairean rebels said on Saturday frontline units had advanced beyond the town of Kenge and were now within 150 km (95 miles) of the capital Kinshasa.
"Our frontline forces entered Kenge last night and many had left early this morning (Saturday) and have advanced to within 150 km reach of Kinshasa," a senior rebel commander told Reuters.
The commander also confirmed the capture of Lisala, birthplace of ailing President Mobutu Sese Seko.
Previous reports had the rebels entering Kenge, 200 km (120 miles) southeast of Kinshasa, after Mobutu's troops left.
The rebels took Kenge after capturing Kikwit and used bridge-laying gear to reach the small town because Mobutu's presidential guard blew up bridges along the way.
Kenga residents said the rebels entered late Friday or early Saturday. One said people turned out to greet them.

The commander said the rebels of Laurent Kabila's Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo-Zaire (ADFL) were on a two-pronged offensive towards Mobutu's jungle palace at Gbadolite near the border with Central African Republic.
"Our forces are moving towards Gbadolite on two routes -- through (the towns of) Gemena and Businga," he said.
Outside Kinshasa, Gbadolite is the only army outpost well equipped with military hardware.
The road from Lisala to Gbadolite is good by Zaire's dilapidated standards after 32 years of Mobutu's rule.

Carved out of tropical forest where once there stood only a village, Mobutu has erected a palace inspired by Versailles, served by an international airport that is long enough to take the supersonic Concorde.
The rebel advances came as South African President Nelson Mandela struggled with difficulty to arrange peace talks at sea between Kabila and Mobutu.

The South Africans said on Saturday that Kabila was finally heading from Angola for the talks aboard the South African navy vessel the Outeniqua, now docked in the Congolese port of Pointe Noire. Mobutu was on land in Pointe Noire.
Kabila says his only objective in the talks is to persuade Mobutu to resign, sparing the bloodshed if and when his army tries to take Kinshasa, a city of some five million people.
But Mobutu has shown no sign he is ready to give up all the power he has enjoyed for more than three decades.
Analysts in the rebel headquarters city of Lubumbashi said the rebels appeared to be bent on forcing Mobutu to surrender or preventing him from returning to Kinshasa.
In Kinshasa, witnesses and security sources said Kabila's rebels were drawing closer to the teeming capital after seizing Lisala and moving beyond Kenge.
Western security sources also said that in the north the rebels were moving towards Gbadolite.
"Lisala has fallen. The rebels are now heading towards Gemena and Gbadolite on foot, by boat and by road," one source told Reuters in the capital. Mobutu was born in Lisala on October 14, 1930.
The rebels themselves say they are massing fighters and weapons much further south in Kikwit for a final push.
Mobutu's ramshackle army has been unable to halt the rebels who now hold three-quarters of the vast state and all the main cities outside Kinshasa.
Even the elite Presidential Guard, drawn from Mobutu's Ngbandi tribe and related ethnic groups from Equateur, have withdrawn in the face of better armed and disciplined rebels.
Kabila has said Mobutu will be well treated if he agrees to give up power.
Political analysts in Kinshasa say the military pressure building around Kinshasa leaves Mobutu with little choice but to surrender power if talks go ahead as planned on board the ship.
